title: Problems: prediction, overfitting, bias and variance

items.prose: A ferry operator forecasts each day's foot passengers, in hundreds. Six training days carried 4, 7, 5, 9, 6 and 11. Four later test days, held back from every fit, carried 8, 6, 10 and 12.

parts.question: The operator forecasts every day with one constant. Which constant gives the smallest training MSE?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Under squared loss the best constant is one particular average of the six days.

byKey.median: You took the median, which minimises absolute error. Squared loss is minimised by the mean.
byKey.midrange: That is halfway between the smallest and largest days. Squared loss is minimised by the mean of all six.

explain.text: Squared loss is smallest at the mean, so the operator forecasts 7 hundred passengers every day. Any other constant adds its squared gap from 7 to the error.

parts.question: Using the constant 7 from part 1, what is its training MSE? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The misses are $-3, 0, -2, 2, -1, 4$; their squares add to 34, and $34/6 \approx 5.667$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each training day's miss from 7, add the squares, then divide by 6.

byKey.n-minus-1: You divided by 5. The mean squared error divides by all 6 days.
byKey.absolute: That averages the sizes of the misses. Square each miss first.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of the squared misses. Divide it by the 6 days.

explain.text: The constant's training MSE, 5.667, is the variance of the six days, dividing by 6. It is scored on the days that chose the constant, so it flatters it.

parts.question: Using the same constant 7, what is its test MSE on the four test days? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The misses are $1, -1, 3, 5$; their squares add to 36, and $36/4 = 9$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep the forecast at 7, square each test day's miss, then average over the 4 days.

byKey.test-mean: You forecast with the test days' own mean, 9. It was not known when the forecast was made; the constant stays at 7.
byKey.carried: You used the median 6.5, part 1's slip. With the mean 7 the misses are 1, $-1$, 3 and 5.
byKey.absolute: That averages the sizes of the misses. Square them first.

explain.text: On the held-out days the same constant scores 9, against 5.667 on the days it was fitted to. The test number is the honest one: it is what the forecast does on days it never saw.

parts.question: An analyst instead fits a polynomial in each day's temperature that passes exactly through all six training days. What is the lowest degree that can do this?

feedback.correct: Degree 5 has $5 + 1 = 6$ coefficients, one per training day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A degree-$d$ polynomial has $d + 1$ coefficients, and each day is one equation to meet.

byKey.six: Degree 6 has 7 coefficients, one more than needed. Six days need six coefficients: degree 5.
byKey.coefficients-short: Degree 4 has only 5 coefficients, one short of the 6 equations.

explain.text: Six days give six equations, and degree 5 has six coefficients to meet them. Its training MSE is then 0. That is interpolation: every wiggle of the six days, noise included, is copied.

parts.question: The degree-5 polynomial scores a test MSE of 31.4 on the four test days. Using the constant's test MSE 9 from part 3, which forecast should the operator keep?

options.text: The constant 7: its test MSE, 9, is far below the polynomial's 31.4
The polynomial: its training MSE is 0, so nothing fits better
options.why: You chose by training error. Zero is guaranteed with six coefficients on six days, and it says nothing about new days.

options.text: Neither: average the two test MSEs and report 20.2
options.why: Averaging scores mixes in a model nobody should use. Keep the one with the lower test MSE.

options.text: Neither can be judged until there are more training days
options.why: Four held-out days already rank them, and the gap is large: 9 against 31.4.

feedback.correct: Right. The constant tests at 9 and the interpolating polynomial at 31.4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rank the two forecasts by their error on the test days alone.

byKey.polynomial: You chose by training error. Zero is guaranteed with six coefficients on six days, and it says nothing about new days.
byKey.average: Averaging scores mixes in a model nobody should use. Keep the one with the lower test MSE.
byKey.more-days: Four held-out days already rank them, and the gap is large: 9 against 31.4.

explain.text: The polynomial scores 0 on the six days it threaded and 31.4 on days it never saw: the far edge of overfitting. The constant is stiff, yet on new days it wins by more than a factor of 3.

items.prose: A bakery chain forecasts a shop's daily sales, in dozens of loaves, with $k$-nearest neighbours on past days. At one query day the true expected sales are 20 and the noise variance is 4. Refitted on five independent training sets, the forecasts for that day are 17, 18, 16, 17, 17 with $k = 20$ and 23, 18, 19, 17, 23 with $k = 1$.

parts.question: What is the squared bias of the $k = 20$ forecast at the query day?

feedback.correct: The five forecasts average $85/5 = 17$, so the bias is $17 - 20 = -3$ and its square is 9.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the five forecasts, subtract the truth 20, then square.

byKey.bias: That is the bias itself, $17 - 20$. Square it.
byKey.size: That is the size of the bias. The question asks for its square.
byKey.variance: That is the variance of the five forecasts. The bias comes from their average, not their spread.

explain.text: Averaging 20 neighbours reaches days unlike the query day, so every refit lands near 17. That gap of $-3$ is bias, with square 9, and refitting cannot remove it.

parts.question: Using the squared bias 9 from part 1, what is the expected test error of the $k = 20$ forecast? Use the variance that divides by 5. Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The deviations from 17 are $0, 1, -1, 0, 0$, so the variance is $2/5 = 0.4$. The error is $9 + 0.4 + 4 = 13.4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the squared bias, the variance of the five forecasts and the noise variance.

byKey.no-noise: You left out the noise. A new day brings its variance of 4 whatever the model.
byKey.ddof1: You divided by 4 for the variance. Here the variance divides by 5.
byKey.carried: You added the bias, 3, without squaring it. The error adds bias squared.

explain.text: Expected test error is noise plus variance plus squared bias: 13.4 here. The $k = 20$ forecast is steady, with variance 0.4, but its bias costs 9.

parts.question: What is the expected test error of the $k = 1$ forecast, again with the variance that divides by 5? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The forecasts average $100/5 = 20$, so the bias is 0. Deviations $3, -2, -1, -3, 3$ give variance $32/5 = 6.4$, and the error is $0 + 6.4 + 4 = 10.4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the mean of the five $k = 1$ forecasts, then the bias squared, the variance and the noise.

byKey.no-noise: That is bias squared plus variance alone. Add the noise variance, 4.
byKey.ddof1: You divided by 4 for the variance. Here it divides by 5: $32/5 = 6.4$.
byKey.carried: That is the $k = 20$ forecast from part 2. Use the five $k = 1$ forecasts.

explain.text: One neighbour copies one past day, noise and all. So the forecasts centre on the truth but scatter widely. The $k = 1$ forecast trades bias for variance and totals 10.4.

parts.question: Treat the $k = 5$ forecast as an average of five neighbours with independent noises, each of variance 4. Its squared bias here is 1. What is its expected test error? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The average of five independent noises has variance $4/5 = 0.8$, so the error is $1 + 0.8 + 4 = 5.8$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the neighbours' noise variance by 5, then add the squared bias and the new day's noise.

byKey.no-average: You kept the variance at 4. Averaging five independent noises divides their variance by 5.
byKey.no-noise: You left out the noise of the new day. It adds 4 whatever the model does.

explain.text: Averaging five neighbours cuts the variance to 0.8 and adds only a little bias, for a total of 5.8. The new day's noise, 4, stays for every $k$.

parts.question: Parts 2 to 4 gave expected errors 13.4, 10.4 and 5.8. Which $k$ should the bakery use on days like this?

options.text: $k = 5$: it balances bias and variance, with the lowest expected error, 5.8
$k = 1$: it has no bias at all
options.why: Zero bias came with variance 6.4. Its total, 10.4, is above 5.8.

options.text: $k = 20$: its forecasts barely move between training sets
options.why: Low variance came with bias squared 9. Its total, 13.4, is the worst of the three.
Every training day is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is 0 for any data. It cannot rank $k$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the three expected test errors and keep the smallest.

byKey.k1: Zero bias came with variance 6.4. Its total, 10.4, is above 5.8.
byKey.k20: Low variance came with bias squared 9. Its total, 13.4, is the worst of the three.
byKey.train: Every training day is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is 0 for any data. It cannot rank $k$.

explain.text: Small $k$ loses on variance and large $k$ on bias; $k = 5$ sits near the bottom of the U. In practice the bakery would find it from test error on held-out days.

items.prose: A broker forecasts a client's next-month commission, in £ hundreds, from trades last month and account value in £ thousands. Across clients, trades have standard deviation 5 and account value 40. Training clients: A (13 trades, £340k, commission 7), B (22, £315k, 3), C (15, £290k, 8) and D (9, £312k, 4). A new client has 14 trades and £310k.

parts.question: On the raw features, what is the Euclidean distance from the new client to D? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The gaps are $14 - 9 = 5$ trades and $310 - 312 = -2$, so the distance is $\sqrt{25 + 4} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.39$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the gap in each feature, add, then take the root.

byKey.squared: That is the squared distance. Take its square root.
byKey.city-block: You added the two gaps. Euclidean distance is the root of the sum of their squares.

explain.text: On raw features D looks like the nearest client, at 5.39, with B next at 9.43. Both are near only because their account values happen to be close.

parts.question: After dividing each feature by its standard deviation, what is the distance from the new client to C? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The scaled gaps are $1/5 = 0.2$ and $20/40 = 0.5$, so the distance is $\sqrt{0.04 + 0.25} = \sqrt{0.29} \approx 0.54$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn each gap into standard deviations, then use Pythagoras.

byKey.raw: That is the raw distance, driven by the £20k gap. Divide each gap by its standard deviation first.
byKey.variance: You divided each gap by the variance. Divide by the standard deviation: 5 for trades, 40 for value.

explain.text: Scaled, C is the nearest client at 0.54 and A next at 0.78. D falls to 1.00 and B to 1.60. The order changes because raw £ thousands outweighed trades.

parts.question: Using the scaled distances, what does 2-NN forecast for the new client, in £ hundreds? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The two nearest scaled clients are C (0.54) and A (0.78), so the forecast is $(8 + 7)/2 = 7.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the two nearest clients on scaled features, then average their commissions.

byKey.raw: You used the raw nearest pair, D and B. On scaled features the nearest are C and A.
byKey.all-four: That averages all four clients. With $k = 2$ only the two nearest count.
byKey.one: That copies the single nearest client, C. Average the two nearest.

explain.text: Scaling turned the forecast from 3.5 to 7.5. Without it the client with the larger units, account value, decided who counted as a neighbour.

parts.question: The new client and two others were held out. Their forecasts were 7.5, 6 and 5, and their commissions turned out to be 7, 6.5 and 4. Using the forecast 7.5 from part 3, what is the test MSE? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The misses are $0.5, -0.5, 1$; their squares add to $0.25 + 0.25 + 1 = 1.5$, and $1.5/3 = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each held-out client's miss, add, then divide by 3.

byKey.carried: You used the raw forecast 3.5, part 3's slip. With 7.5 the misses are 0.5, $-0.5$ and 1.
byKey.absolute: That averages the sizes of the misses. Square them first.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of the squared misses. Divide by the 3 clients.

explain.text: The three clients took no part in the fit, so 0.5 estimates the error on new clients. A score on the training clients would flatter the model.

parts.question: The four training commissions have mean 5.5. What test MSE does forecasting 5.5 for all three held-out clients score? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The misses are $1.5, 1, -1.5$; their squares add to $2.25 + 1 + 2.25 = 5.5$, and $5.5/3 \approx 1.833$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Forecast 5.5 for each held-out client, square the misses, then average.

byKey.test-mean: You used the held-out clients' own mean. It was not known when the forecasts were made; the baseline is the training mean, 5.5.
byKey.absolute: That averages the sizes of the misses. Square them first.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of the squared misses. Divide by the 3 clients.

explain.text: The training mean is the best constant a forecaster could have known in advance. Scaled 2-NN scores 0.5 against its 1.833 on the same clients, so the features carry real information.

items.prose: A district heating firm forecasts a day's heat demand from the outdoor temperature with polynomials. Each is fitted on 40 training days and scored on 40 later days. Training and test MSE, in MWh², by degree: 0 (9.20, 9.85), 1 (3.10, 3.42), 2 (1.44, 1.80), 3 (1.38, 1.95) and 6 (1.02, 2.60). The noise variance is 1.20.

parts.question: Which degree should the firm keep?

feedback.correct: Degree 2 has the lowest test MSE, 1.80.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rank the degrees by test MSE alone.

byKey.training: Degree 6 has the lowest training MSE, 1.02, the number that lies. Its test MSE, 2.60, is worse than degree 2's.
byKey.next: Degree 3 fits the training days a little better, but tests at 1.95, above degree 2's 1.80.

explain.text: Training MSE falls at every degree, from 9.20 to 1.02, so it cannot choose. Test MSE bottoms out at degree 2, then climbs as the curve starts fitting noise.

parts.question: Treat each test MSE as its expected value: noise plus squared bias plus variance, averaged over the test days. Using degree 2's test MSE 1.80, what do its squared bias and variance add up to? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the noise variance away from degree 2's test MSE.

byKey.training: You used degree 2's training MSE, 1.44. The decomposition is of the error on new days.
byKey.carried: You used degree 6's test MSE, 2.60. The kept degree is 2, at 1.80.
byKey.added: You added the noise. Take it away: the noise is part of the 1.80.

explain.text: No model removes the 1.20 of noise. What degree 2 can still improve is the 0.60 above it, split between bias and variance.

parts.question: Refits on 200 training sets put degree 2's variance at 0.36. Using 0.60 from part 2, what is its squared bias? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Squared bias is the 0.60 less the variance.

byKey.sd: You treated 0.36 as a standard deviation and squared it. It is already the variance.
byKey.carried: You started from 1.40, degree 6's part. Degree 2 has 0.60 above the noise.
byKey.added: You added the variance. The squared bias is what is left once it is taken away.

explain.text: Degree 2 carries squared bias 0.24 and variance 0.36. More data shrinks only the second.

parts.question: Suppose variance falls in proportion to $1/n$. With 400 training days instead of 40, what is degree 2's expected test MSE? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Ten times the days cut the variance to $0.36/10 = 0.036$, so the error is $1.20 + 0.24 + 0.036 = 1.476$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the variance by 10, keep the squared bias, and add the noise.

byKey.all-shrink: You shrank the bias too. Only the variance falls with more data; the squared bias stays 0.24.
byKey.no-noise: You left out the noise, 1.20. It stays whatever the data.
byKey.carried: You used the squared bias 1.04, part 3's slip. Degree 2's is 0.24.

explain.text: Degree 2 falls from 1.80 to 1.476 but no further than $1.20 + 0.24 = 1.44$, however many days it sees. Its bias is the floor above the noise.

parts.question: For degree 6 the refits give squared bias 0.02 at 40 days. With 400 days and the same $1/n$ rule, what is degree 6's expected test MSE? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find degree 6's variance at 40 days, divide it by 10, then add the squared bias and the noise.

byKey.no-shrink: That is degree 6 at 40 days. With ten times the data its variance falls by 10.
byKey.all-shrink: You shrank the bias too. Only the variance, 1.38, falls by 10.

explain.text: With 400 days degree 6 tests at 1.358, below degree 2's 1.476. More data tames variance, so the best degree moves up; it never removes bias.
